name: PowerView - Test-AdminAccess (Local Admin Check)
description: Tests whether the current user context has local administrator access on a remote host by attempting to open the SCM (Service Control Manager) with admin rights. Returns True/False quickly for each target. Used after obtaining credentials to efficiently check which machines you can move to without triggering excessive network noise.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHAT TEST-ADMINACCESS DOES ===
Attempts to open the Windows Service Control Manager (SCM) on the remote host
with SC_MANAGER_ALL_ACCESS rights. This is a standard WMI/RPC call that:
  - Returns TRUE if current user is a local admin on the target
  - Returns FALSE if access denied
  - Does NOT execute code on the target — just a permission check

Event generated: 4624 (logon) + 4634 (logoff) on the TARGET — detectable but brief.
CrackMapExec --local-auth --check-admin does the same thing at scale.

=== USE CASE IN THE ATTACK CHAIN ===
Typical scenario:
  1. Crack an NTLMv2 hash → get a password for jsmith
  2. You don't know which machines jsmith is a local admin on
  3. Run Test-AdminAccess against all live hosts to find your pivot points
  4. Move to those hosts via Evil-WinRM, PSExec, etc.

=== SCAN ACROSS ALL DOMAIN COMPUTERS ===
Get-DomainComputer | Select Name | ForEach-Object {
    $result = Test-AdminAccess -ComputerName $_.Name
    [PSCustomObject]@{Computer=$_.Name; AdminAccess=$result.IsAdmin}
}
This finds every machine where your current creds have local admin.

=== CAVEATS ===
  - Works best in the context of the compromised credential (run as that user via runas or PSCredential)
  - If you're running as a different user, results reflect your actual session
  - WFW (Windows Firewall) can block the RPC call — machine looks like 'access denied' but really just firewalled
  - CrackMapExec --check alternative: cme smb <subnet> -u user -p pass → shows Pwn3d! status Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 21 (Active Directory Introduction and Enumeration).

examples.label: Sweep all domain computers
examples.command: Get-DomainComputer | Select -ExpandProperty Name | ForEach-Object { if((Test-AdminAccess -ComputerName $_).IsAdmin) { Write-Host "ADMIN: $_" } }

examples.label: Ch21 — Find-LocalAdminAccess (returns hostnames where current user is local admin)

defense.why_it_works: Test-AdminAccess (PowerView) checks which hosts the current user has local admin on, finding lateral-movement footholds.
defense.prerequisites: Domain credentials and SMB reachability to the target hosts.
defense.impact: A list of hosts where the current creds are local admin.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1087.002] Broad/bulk LDAP queries to the DC (Event 4662 directory-service access; Microsoft Defender for Identity reconnaissance alerts); one host reading large swaths of the directory in a short window.
defense.artifacts: SMB/RPC access checks across hosts (fan-out) plus LDAP host enumeration.
defense.prevention: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design, so prevention is limited - focus on DETECTION (Defender for Identity, LDAP/SMB anomaly monitoring), least privilege, disabling anonymous/null sessions, and REDUCING what's exposed (remove unnecessary SPNs, descriptions with secrets, over-shared folders).
defense.evasion: Use built-in tools (net, AD module, dsquery) that blend with normal admin activity; throttle and scope collection; avoid the noisiest methods (full BloodHound sweeps, RID brute) where Defender for Identity is present.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects

steps.label: Find where your user is local admin
